article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: QTEL approach: rigorous academic content and academic English taught simultaneously with expert support
description: The Quality Teaching for English Learners (QTEL) initiative holds that secondary ELL students can master rigorous academic content quickly and deeply rather than waiting years to learn English mechanics first. It works on the premise that students will rise to the challenge of rigorous subject matter if it sparks their interest, if they receive appropriate support, and if academic content and academic English language skills are taught simultaneously, as a single, integrated process. The article presents this as a counter to the traditional belief that ELL students need seven years of English before tackling complex academic content.
requirements: Teachers must make dramatic shifts in their beliefs and practices to master this instructional approach
target_learners: middle school and high school English language learners at intermediate English proficiency
target_learning_goals: academic English listening, speaking, reading, and writing
examples: The Persuasion across Time and Space unit was piloted in five urban school districts through a partnership between the Understanding Language initiative at Stanford and WestEd's Teacher Professional Development Program.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: The Impact of Quantum Teaching Strategy on Student Academic Achievements and Self-Esteem in Inclusive Schools
citation: Gunarhadi, Mustapa Kassim & Abdull Sukor Shaari. (2014). THE IMPACT OF QUANTUM TEACHING STRATEGY ON STUDENT ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENTS AND SELF-ESTEEM IN INCLUSIVE SCHOOLS. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction: Vol. 11 (2014): 191-205. http://mjli.uum.edu.my/
title: Quantum Teaching content sequence: enroll, experience, demonstrate, and celebrate
description: The content element of Quantum Teaching follows a five-step lesson sequence proposed by DePorter (1992). The teacher first "enroll"s students to capture interest, curiosity, and attention; then has them "experience" content through exploration, which the article says better maintains long-term memory than reading or listening, followed by discussion, verification, and labeling of concepts; then students "demonstrate" their capability, followed by reflection and repetition to strengthen nerve connections; and finally the class "celebrate"s to appreciate those who finished tasks successfully, providing new energy for upcoming learning.
requirements: Exploration activities followed by discussion, verification, and labeling of discovered concepts
Reflection and repetition after demonstration to strengthen nerve connections
constraints: The article presents this sequence as part of the Quantum Teaching framework rather than as an independently tested component
target_learners: sixth-grade students in inclusive elementary schools
target_learning_goals: content mastery in Bahasa Indonesia and Science
student confidence through demonstration and celebration
examples: In the study, the content element was implemented through integrated themes: language skills through drama for Bahasa Indonesia and natural environment for Science
key_sources: Gunarhadi, Mustapa Kassim & Abdull Sukor Shaari. (2014). THE IMPACT OF QUANTUM TEACHING STRATEGY ON STUDENT ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENTS AND SELF-ESTEEM IN INCLUSIVE SCHOOLS. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction: Vol. 11 (2014): 191-205. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1137291

article_title: The Impact of Quantum Teaching Strategy on Student Academic Achievements and Self-Esteem in Inclusive Schools
citation: Gunarhadi, Mustapa Kassim & Abdull Sukor Shaari. (2014). THE IMPACT OF QUANTUM TEACHING STRATEGY ON STUDENT ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENTS AND SELF-ESTEEM IN INCLUSIVE SCHOOLS. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction: Vol. 11 (2014): 191-205. http://mjli.uum.edu.my/
title: Quantum Teaching context orchestration: atmosphere, foundation, environment, and lesson design
description: The context element of Quantum Teaching assigns the teacher to orchestrate four aspects of the classroom learning setting. First, orchestrating the learning atmosphere creates intimacy, warmth, humor, and accountability with positive emotional bonds between teachers and students. Second, orchestrating a strong foundation commits teachers to learning behaviors aligned with positive values and lifelong learning. Third, orchestrating the learning environment makes it safe, comfortable, and fun. Fourth, orchestrating the lesson plan prepares students for success through strategies bridging teaching materials and students' prior knowledge.
requirements: Teacher commitment to creating learning behaviors in accordance with positive values inherent in students
Managing the learning environment to make it safe, comfortable, and fun to learn
constraints: The article presents this as the framework's context element rather than as an independently tested component
target_learners: sixth-grade students in inclusive elementary schools, including children with special needs
target_learning_goals: academic success through bridging prior knowledge
examples: The article contrasts this with conventional teaching characterized by fixed seating arrangement, a textbook approach, and teacher-dominated learning environments

article_title: Quantum Technology masters: A shortcut to the quantum industry?
citation: Simon Goorney, Borja Muñoz, Jacob Sherson. (2024). Quantum Technology master’s: A shortcut to the quantum industry? https://digiq.eu/
title: Dataset of 86 QT master's programs with career-outcome text corpus (D1 coordinator survey and D2 website text analysis)
description: A compiled dataset of Quantum Technology master's programs worldwide, recording country, city, program name, website link, first student entry, responsible faculties, internship offerings, and expected career outcomes. Program information "was verified with the program coordinators or representatives of each master's program through email". The career-outcome component (D2) processed 46 website documents with Voyant tools, yielding a final list of 42 unique words and 111 occurrences classified across 14 distinct career destinations. The majority of data sources are available in the article's Appendices.
requirements: Program information verified with program coordinators or representatives through email
constraints: Data obtained through email survey is provided in aggregate for privacy protection
target_learners: prospective and enrolled QT master's students
target_learning_goals: understanding career destinations and program structure in Quantum Technology higher education
examples: The D2 analysis used Voyant tools on 46 documents containing 721 unique words and 2583 occurrences, reduced after stopword removal to 42 unique words and 111 occurrences across 14 career destinations.
key_sources: Simon Goorney, Borja Muñoz, Jacob Sherson. (2024). Quantum Technology master’s: A shortcut to the quantum industry? https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07497

article_title: QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics
citation: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430
title: QTris: a tic-tac-toe-based board game whose sequences simulate quantum processes on a system of nine qubits
description: QTris (Quantum Tris) is a variant of tic-tac-toe for two players (white and black) on a 3x3 grid, with three phases: preparation (placing four tile types), operations (playing move cards I, X, Y, Z, H), and measurement (rolling a die to measure color with rule-book probabilities). The basic idea is that "each cell of the grid represents a single qubit, so that the whole board represents a system of nine qubits", so every game sequence simulates a quantum experiment or calculation. The previous version's rules can be downloaded for free.
requirements: Rule-book giving measurement probabilities for each state; a d100 (or two d10s) for the measurement phase; move cards
constraints: In the basic version the final measurement is always a color measurement; points are scored only after the measurement phase
target_learning_goals: understanding probabilistic measurement, unitary transformation, incompatibility, and state superposition in Quantum Mechanics
examples: A complete example game is given with preparation, five operation turns, and a measurement phase ending in a 1-1 draw
key_sources: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430

article_title: QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics
citation: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430
title: Four-level structural analogy between QTris and qubit Quantum Mechanics: observables, states, unitary operations, measurement
description: The article defines a structural analogy between QTris (basic version) and QM for qubit systems, summarized in Table 1 at four levels: observables (Color and Orientation analogous to maximally incompatible observables Z and X), states (color-tiles and orientation-tiles as eigenstates {|0>,|1>} and {|+>,|->}), unitary operations (move cards I, X, Y, Z, H analogous to Pauli operators plus Hadamard), and measurement (die-roll probabilities analogous to the Born Rule for a Z measurement). By this analogy, game problems can be framed as typical QM problems in disguise, translatable into Dirac notation.
requirements: All new states and operations must be defined without ambiguities or contradictions for the analogy to extend
constraints: The correspondence between game elements and the QM mathematical framework partially breaks down at some points, discussed in the article's extensions section
target_learning_goals: understanding observables, eigenstates, unitary operations, and the Born Rule for two-state systems
examples: A game sequence preparing |0>, applying X then H, and measuring Z is shown equivalent to the corresponding quantum process with probabilities 1/2 and 1/2
key_sources: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430

article_title: QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics
citation: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430
title: Entanglement extension of QTris via the Controlled-X card and triangular-tile Bell states
description: Entanglement is introduced into QTris by the Controlled-X card (C X), "analogous to the CNOT gate of quantum computers"; it is the only card acting on two cells at once, with control and target roles. Applying C X to certain control-target combinations generates four new two-cell entangled states represented by couples of signed triangular tiles, characterized by global properties of Alignment and Sign, whose color is completely unpredictable. Measurement rules give each possible result with probability 1/2, and X and Z operations change Alignment and Sign respectively.
requirements: Rules for operations and color measurements on triangular states must be defined; the player must choose which cell acts as control when disentangling
constraints: A further extension introducing a third basis of Y eigenstates is deferred to a future work
target_learning_goals: understanding entanglement and its distinction from classical correlations
examples: Using C X twice with inverted control and target roles can swap the positions of two tiles on the board
key_sources: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430

article_title: QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics
citation: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430
title: QTris as a formally well-defined sequential quantum game within Quantum Game Theory
description: The article situates QTris within Quantum Game Theory (QGT), an extension of Classical Game Theory in which classical information carriers are replaced by quantum systems. QTris satisfies the criteria identifying a quantum game: the board represents a quantum register defining the Hilbert space, the preparation phase corresponds to the initial quantum state, the cards define the admissible quantum operations, and the final measurement determines payoffs. The authors conclude that "QTris is a formally well defined sequential quantum game whose dynamics can be analyzed within the general framework of QGT."
requirements: A Hilbert space, an initial quantum state, a set of admissible quantum operations, and a measurement procedure determining outcome probabilities and payoffs
constraints: Sequential quantum games introduce an explicit temporal structure, unlike most cited protocol-based formulations which focused on simultaneous games
target_learning_goals: understanding strategic interactions involving quantum resources such as superposition and entanglement
examples: The article traces QGT origins to Meyer's demonstration that quantum strategies may outperform classical ones in suitable strategic settings
key_sources: Amabile, A., Bondani, M., De Simone, I., Nazzaro, M., Viscardi, M., Hamma, A. (2026). QTris: a pedagogical board game to teach Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09430
